title: ChatGPT in physics education: A pilot study on easy-to-implement activities
extended_summary:
This paper explores how ChatGPT can be used in secondary physics education to support critical thinking and classroom discussion. The author argues that large language models have educational potential, but also notable risks and limitations, including biased or incorrect outputs and the need for students to critically evaluate AI-generated text.

The paper presents two easy-to-implement classroom activities centered on quantum physics. In the first, students generate ChatGPT responses about photons, critique their scientific accuracy and clarity, compare answers across prompts, and revise the text using additional sources. In the second, students use ChatGPT to create a short conceptual survey on wave-particle duality, check the items for validity, and discuss the results with peers. The activities are framed as tools for fostering student reflection on both the benefits and pitfalls of ChatGPT.

A pilot field study tested the approach in two 12th-grade physics classes at a German Gymnasium. The intervention consisted of two 45-minute lessons taught by an instructed teacher during regular physics instruction. Using a one-group pretest-posttest design and a questionnaire on students’ perceptions of AI and ChatGPT, the study found generally more favorable post-intervention views of ChatGPT, including stronger agreement that it should be incorporated into daily life and can be useful for learning tasks. The author concludes that the activities may positively shape student perceptions of ChatGPT, while emphasizing that more research is needed on long-term effects and on how ChatGPT can be integrated into classroom practice.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's generative pre-trained transformer chatbot for conversational text generation and other natural-language tasks.
identified_tools.use_case: Used in two easy-to-implement classroom activities for secondary physics: students generated and critically analyzed ChatGPT outputs, and students used ChatGPT to create a three-item conceptual survey on quantum physics for peer discussion. The paper also reports a pilot field implementation of these activities in two 12th-grade physics classes.

findings.finding_summary: In a one-group pretest-posttest pilot with two 12th-grade physics classes (n=53), students' perceptions of ChatGPT improved after a two-lesson intervention. Agreement increased for several ChatGPT items, including belief that it should be incorporated into daily life (M=3.53 to 4.60), that benefits outweigh harms (M=3.13 to 4.45), and that it helps accomplish tasks more quickly (M=3.42 to 4.38).
findings.measure: Students' perceptions of the importance/benefits of ChatGPT on a 9-item 5-point questionnaire

findings.finding_summary: One ChatGPT-related item moved in the opposite direction: agreement with the statement that students can use ChatGPT even if they do not understand how it works decreased from M=3.32 (SD=1.32) to M=2.66 (SD=0.95). The authors interpret this as possible increased awareness that outputs should not be consumed uncritically, but they do not report statistical significance.
findings.measure: Agreement with the statement that ChatGPT can be used without understanding how it works

quality_tier_rationale: This is a small one-group pretest-posttest pilot study with no control group and no inferential statistics reported, so internal validity is limited. It still provides direct classroom field evidence on repeated use of ChatGPT by students and a teacher-led implementation.
impact_tier_rationale: The reported changes are modest to positive in student perceptions, but no effect sizes are given and the design does not support strong causal claims. The study does include a potentially informative negative/critical-awareness signal on one item, but not evidence of harm or no effect.
